title: Given n nodes and a list of undirected edges, count the number of connected components using Union-Find.
shortTitle: Number of Connected Components — union nodes, count roots

s1_definition.profdef: The number of connected components equals the number of distinct roots remaining after unioning every edge. Starting with n singleton sets, each edge that joins two previously separate sets reduces the component count by one; edges within an already-joined set change nothing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has n branches with no links. Each new settlement cable connects two branches. Whenever a cable joins two branches that were not yet in the same network, the number of separate networks drops by one. At the end, the number of independent networks is your component count.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start with n components and subtract one for every edge that merges two different sets — what's left is the count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The number of connected components equals the number of distinct roots remaining after unioning every edge. Starting with n singleton sets, each edge that joins two previously separate sets reduces the component count by one; edges within an already-joined set change nothing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has n branches with no links. Each new settlement cable connects two branches. Whenever a cable joins two branches that were not yet in the same network, the number of separate networks drops by one. At the end, the number of independent networks is your component count.

**One line to remember:** Start with n components and subtract one for every edge that merges two different sets — what's left is the count.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize Union-Find with n elements and a counter set to n. For each edge, call union on its endpoints; a successful union decrements the counter. For example: `if (uf.union(u, v)) components--;`.

An edge that connects two nodes already in the same set returns false and leaves the counter unchanged, because it adds no new connectivity. For example: `union(2, 3)` when two and three are already linked does nothing to the count.

The final answer is simply the remaining counter value, which equals the number of distinct roots. The time is the number of edges times the near-constant union cost, and the space is the parent and rank arrays.

A senior nuance is that this is strictly faster to reason about than a DFS flood-fill when edges stream in incrementally, because Union-Find answers the running count online without re-traversing the graph.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, branches are connected by settlement links and operations need to know how many independent settlement networks currently exist, because each isolated network needs its own reconciliation batch. This is exactly how counting connected components works.

Problem 2 — When a link is added between two branches already in the same network, nothing changes; the count must not drop. This is exactly why a union only decrements on a real merge.

The mini-project builds a `SettlementNetworkCounter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five branches and three links.

Step 1: The counter starts at five, with every branch its own network.

Step 2: Link zero-one merges two networks, dropping the count to four.

Step 3: Link one-two merges branch two into the growing network, dropping the count to three.

Step 4: Link three-four merges those two branches, dropping the count to two.

Step 5: No link falls within an existing network here, so the final count is two: the set zero-one-two and the set three-four.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting connected components with Union-Find is a clean online algorithm: I start with a component counter equal to the number of nodes, because every node begins as its own isolated set, and I process each edge by attempting a union of its endpoints. The key detail is that I only decrement the counter when a union actually merges two previously separate sets. An edge between two nodes that already share a root changes nothing, so the counter correctly ignores it.

At the end, the counter holds the number of distinct roots, which is exactly the number of connected components. The cost is the number of edges times the near-constant Union-Find operation cost, and it uses only the parent and rank arrays, so it is both fast and memory-light.

In my project at National Bank of India, operations needed to know how many independent settlement networks existed among the branches, because each isolated network required its own reconciliation batch. Union-Find let me maintain that count online as links were added, and because a redundant link never dropped the count, the number of reconciliation batches stayed correct without ever re-traversing the whole topology.
